Some of those standing there said to them, “What are you doing, untying the colt?”
They answered them just as Jesus had said, and the people let them go.
They brought the colt to Jesus, threw their garments on it, and He sat on it.
Many spread their garments on the road; others spread leafy branches they had cut from the fields.
Those going ahead and those following cried out, “Hosanna! Blessed is the One who comes in the name of the Lord!
Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!”
He entered Jerusalem, into the temple. After looking around at everything, since the hour was already late, He went out to Bethany with the Twelve.
On the next day, as they came out from Bethany, He became hungry.
Seeing from far away a fig tree with leaves, He came to see whether He might find anything on it. When He reached it, He found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.
He addressed it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” His disciples heard it.
They came to Jerusalem. He entered the temple and began driving out those selling and those buying in the temple. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves,
and would not allow anyone to carry a vessel through the temple.
He taught and said to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.”
The chief priests and the scribes heard, and sought how to destroy Him; for they feared Him, because the whole crowd was astonished at His teaching.
Whenever evening came, they went out of the city.
Passing by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered from the roots.
Peter remembered and said to Him, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree that Thou didst curse has withered.”
Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God.
Truly I tell you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says is happening, it will be his.
Therefore I tell you, everything you pray and ask for—believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
Whenever you stand praying, forgive if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father in the heavens may also forgive your trespasses.”
They came again to Jerusalem. As He walked in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders came to Him
and said to Him, “By what authority art Thou doing these things? Or who gave Thee this authority to do them?”
Jesus said to them, “I will ask you one question. Answer Me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things.
Was John’s baptism from heaven or from humans? Answer Me.”
They reasoned with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’
But should we say, ‘From humans’?” They feared the crowd, for everyone held that John truly was a prophet.
They answered Jesus, “We do not know.” Jesus said to them, “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things.”
He began speaking to them in parables: “A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a winepress vat, and built a tower. He leased it to tenant farmers and went abroad.
At the proper season he sent a slave to the farmers, to receive from them some of the vineyard’s fruit.
They seized him, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.
Again he sent another slave to them; they struck that one on the head and dishonored him.
He sent another, and they killed that one; and many others—some they beat, and others they killed.
He still had one, a beloved son. He sent him to them last, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
But those farmers said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’
They seized him, killed him, and threw him outside the vineyard.
What, then, will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the farmers and give the vineyard to others.
Have you not even read this Scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
This came from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?”
They sought to seize Him, but feared the crowd, for they knew that He had spoken the parable against them. They left Him and went away.
They sent some of the Pharisees and the Herodians to Him, to catch Him in a word.

They came and said to Him, “Teacher, we know that Thou art truthful and dost not defer to anyone, for Thou dost not look at people’s outward standing, but dost teach God’s way in truth. Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not? Should we give it or not?”
Knowing their hypocrisy, He said to them, “Why are you testing Me? Bring Me a denarius so that I may see it.”
They brought one. He said to them, “Whose image and inscription is this?” They said to Him, “Caesar’s.”
Jesus said to them, “Give back Caesar’s things to Caesar, and God’s things to God.” They marveled greatly at Him.
Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to Him and questioned Him, saying,
“Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if someone’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no child, his brother should take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.
There were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died leaving no offspring.
The second took her and died leaving no offspring, and the third likewise.
The seven left no offspring. Last of all, the woman also died.
In the resurrection, when they rise, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife.”
Jesus said to them, “Is this not why you are mistaken: you know neither the Scriptures nor God’s power?
For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in the heavens.
As for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’?
He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are greatly mistaken.”
One of the scribes approached, having heard them disputing and seen that He had answered them well. He asked Him, “Which commandment is first of all?”
Jesus answered, “The first is, ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.
You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, with your whole mind, and with your whole strength.’
The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”
The scribe said to Him, “Well said, Teacher! Thou hast truly said that He is one, and there is no other besides Him.
To love Him with the whole heart, with the whole understanding, and with the whole strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.”
Seeing that he answered thoughtfully, Jesus said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” No one dared to question Him any further.
Jesus responded as He taught in the temple, “How do the scribes say that the Christ is David’s son?
David himself said in the Holy Spirit, ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at My right hand until I put Thy enemies beneath Thy feet.’
David himself calls Him Lord; how then is He his son?” The large crowd listened to Him gladly.
In His teaching He said, “Beware of the scribes who like to walk about in long robes and receive greetings in the marketplaces,
the foremost seats in the synagogues, and the foremost reclining places at dinners.
They devour widows’ houses and make long prayers as a pretense. These will receive greater judgment.”
He sat opposite the treasury and watched how the crowd put copper money into the treasury. Many rich people put in much.
And one poor widow came and put in two lepta, which make a quadrans.
He called His disciples to Him and said to them, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those putting into the treasury.
For they all put in from their surplus, but she, from her need, put in everything she had—her whole livelihood.”
As He was leaving the temple, one of His disciples said to Him, “Teacher, look! What stones and what buildings!”
Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? Not one stone will be left here on another that will not be torn down.”
As He sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew questioned Him privately:
“Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be fulfilled?”
Jesus began saying to them, “Watch out that no one leads you astray.
Many will come in My name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and will lead many astray.
When you hear of wars and reports of wars, do not be alarmed. These must happen, but the end is not yet.
For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These things are the beginning of birth pains.
But watch yourselves. They will hand you over to councils; you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for My sake, as a testimony to them.
The gospel must first be proclaimed to all the nations.
When they lead you away to hand you over, do not worry beforehand about what to say. Whatever is given you in that hour, say that; for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.
Brother will hand brother over to death, and a father his child. Children will rise against parents and have them put to death.
You will be hated by all because of My name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
When you see the abomination of desolation standing where it must not—let the reader understand—then let those in Judea flee to the mountains.
Let the one on the housetop not go down or enter to take anything from his house,
and let the one in the field not turn back to take his garment.
Woe to those who are pregnant and those nursing infants in those days!
Pray that it does not happen in winter.
For those days will be distress such as has not occurred from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and certainly will not occur again.
If the Lord had not shortened the days, no flesh would have been saved. But for the sake of the chosen, whom He chose, He shortened the days.
Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or, ‘Look, there!’ do not believe it.
For false christs and false prophets will arise and give signs and wonders to lead astray, if possible, the chosen.
But you, watch out! I have told you everything beforehand.
But in those days, after that distress, the sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light.
The stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.
Then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.
Then He will send the angels and gather His chosen from the four winds, from the end of the earth to the end of heaven.
Learn the parable from the fig tree: when its branch has already become tender and puts out leaves, you know that summer is near.
So also, when you see these things happening, know that it is near, at the doors.
Truly I tell you, this generation will certainly not pass away until all these things happen.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will certainly not pass away.
But concerning that day or hour, no one knows—not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son—except the Father.
Watch out; stay awake, for you do not know when the time is.
It is like a man going abroad who left his house and gave his slaves authority, each his own work, and commanded the doorkeeper to keep watch.
Therefore keep watch, for you do not know when the master of the house is coming: in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning.
Otherwise he may come suddenly and find you sleeping.
What I say to you, I say to all: keep watch!”
The Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread were two days away. The chief priests and the scribes sought how to seize Him by deceit and kill Him.
For they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be a disturbance among the people.”
While He was in Bethany, reclining in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came with an alabaster jar of very costly ointment of pure nard. She broke the alabaster jar and poured it over His head.
Some were indignant among themselves: “Why has this ointment been wasted?
For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.” They scolded her harshly.
Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why are you troubling her? She has done a good work for Me.
For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good to them; but you do not always have Me.
She did what she could. She has anointed My body beforehand for burial.
Truly I tell you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in remembrance of her.”
Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went away to the chief priests to hand Him over to them.
When they heard, they rejoiced and promised to give him silver money. He sought how to hand Him over at a suitable time.
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover, His disciples said to Him, “Where dost Thou want us to go and prepare the Passover for Thee to eat?”
He sent two of His disciples and said to them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying an earthenware jar of water will meet you. Follow him.
Wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says: Where is My guest room, where I may eat the Passover with My disciples?’
He will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready. Prepare for us there.”
The disciples went out, came to the city, and found it just as He had told them. They prepared the Passover.
When evening came, He arrived with the Twelve.
As they reclined and ate, Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, one of you will hand Me over—one who is eating with Me.”
They began to be grieved and said to Him one by one, “Surely not I?”
He said to them, “One of the Twelve, the one dipping with Me into the dish.
For the Son of Man goes just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is handed over! It would have been good for that man if he had not been born.”
As they ate, He took bread, pronounced a blessing, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, “Take; this is My body.”
He took a cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, and they all drank from it.
He said to them, “This is My blood of the covenant, poured out for many.
Truly I tell you, I will certainly no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.”
After singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Jesus said to them, “You will all stumble, because it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’
But after I am raised, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”
Peter said to Him, “Even if all stumble, I will not.”
Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you, today, this very night, before a rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.”
He spoke all the more insistently, “Even if I must die with Thee, I will certainly not deny Thee.” They all said the same.
They came to a place whose name was Gethsemane. He said to His disciples, “Sit here while I pray.”
He took Peter, James, and John with Him, and began to be deeply alarmed and distressed.
He said to them, “My soul is deeply grieved, to the point of death. Remain here and keep watch.”
Going forward a little, He fell on the ground and prayed that, if possible, the hour might pass from Him.
He said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for Thee. Take this cup away from Me. Yet not what I will, but what Thou wilt.”
He came and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, “Simon, are you sleeping? Could you not keep watch for one hour?
Keep watch and pray, so that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
Again He went away and prayed, saying the same word.
Again He came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were weighed down, and they did not know what to answer Him.
He came the third time and said to them, “Sleep on now and rest. It is enough. The hour has come. Look, the Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners.
Rise; let us go. Look, the one handing Me over has drawn near.”
Immediately, while He was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs from the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders.
The one handing Him over had given them an agreed sign, saying, “The One I kiss is He. Seize Him and lead Him away securely.”
He came and immediately approached Him, saying, “Rabbi!” Then he kissed Him.
They laid their hands on Him and seized Him.
One of those standing nearby drew his sword, struck the high priest’s slave, and cut off his ear.
Jesus answered them, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as though against a robber?
Day after day I was with you in the temple, teaching, and you did not seize Me. But this is so that the Scriptures may be fulfilled.”
They all left Him and fled.
A certain young man was following Him, wearing a linen cloth over his naked body. They seized him,
but he left the linen cloth behind and fled naked.
They led Jesus away to the high priest, and all the chief priests, the elders, and the scribes assembled.
Peter followed Him from a distance, as far as inside the high priest’s courtyard. He sat with the attendants and warmed himself at the firelight.
The chief priests and the whole council sought testimony against Jesus to put Him to death, but found none.
For many bore false witness against Him, but their testimonies did not agree.
Some stood up and bore false witness against Him, saying,
“We heard Him say, ‘I will tear down this sanctuary made by hands, and in three days I will build another not made by hands.’”
Yet even in this their testimony did not agree.
The high priest stood up in the midst and questioned Jesus, saying, “Dost Thou answer nothing? What is it these men testify against Thee?”
He remained silent and answered nothing. Again the high priest questioned Him and said to Him, “Art Thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?”
Jesus said, “I am. And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right of the Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”
The high priest tore his tunics and said, “What further need have we of witnesses?
You heard the blasphemy. What is your judgment?” They all condemned Him as deserving death.
Some began spitting on Him, covering His face, striking Him with their fists, and saying to Him, “Prophesy!” The attendants received Him with slaps.
While Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s female slaves came.
Seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, “You too were with Jesus the Nazarene.”
He denied it, saying, “I neither know nor understand what you are saying.” He went outside into the forecourt, and a rooster crowed.
The female slave saw him and again began saying to those standing nearby, “This man is one of them.”
Again he denied it. After a little while, those standing nearby again said to Peter, “Truly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean.”
He began invoking a curse and swearing, “I do not know this Man you are speaking of.”
Immediately a rooster crowed a second time. Peter remembered the word Jesus had spoken to him: “Before a rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” He broke down and wept.
Immediately in the morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders, the scribes, and the whole council. They bound Jesus, led Him away, and handed Him over to Pilate.
Pilate questioned Him, “Art Thou the King of the Jews?” He answered him, “You say so.”
The chief priests accused Him of many things.
Pilate questioned Him again, saying, “Dost Thou answer nothing? Look how many accusations they bring against Thee.”
But Jesus gave no further answer, so that Pilate marveled.
At the feast he used to release for them one prisoner whom they requested.
The man called Barabbas was imprisoned with the rebels who had committed murder in the uprising.
The crowd came up and began asking him to do as he usually did for them.
Pilate answered them, “Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?”
For he knew that the chief priests had handed Him over out of envy.
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas for them instead.
Pilate answered them again, “Then what do you want me to do with the One you call the King of the Jews?”
They cried out again, “Crucify Him!”
Pilate said to them, “Why, what evil has He done?” They cried out all the more, “Crucify Him!”
Pilate, wanting to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas for them. After having Jesus scourged, he handed Him over to be crucified.
The soldiers led Him inside the courtyard—that is, the praetorium—and called together the whole cohort.
They clothed Him in purple and, after weaving a crown of thorns, put it on Him.
They began saluting Him, “Hail, King of the Jews!”
They kept striking His head with a reed and spitting on Him, and knelt down to bow before Him.
After they had mocked Him, they stripped off the purple and put His own garments on Him. They led Him out to crucify Him.
They compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, coming from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry His cross.
They brought Him to the place Golgotha, which translated means Place of a Skull.
They offered Him wine mixed with myrrh, but He did not take it.
They crucified Him and divided His garments, casting a lot over them to determine who would take what.
It was the third hour when they crucified Him.
The inscription of the charge against Him was written: “The King of the Jews.”
They crucified two robbers with Him, one at His right and one at His left.
Those passing by reviled Him, shaking their heads and saying, “Aha! Thou who dost tear down the sanctuary and build it in three days,
save Thyself by coming down from the cross!”
Likewise the chief priests, mocking Him among themselves with the scribes, said, “He saved others; He cannot save Himself.
Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe.” Those crucified with Him also reproached Him.
When the sixth hour came, darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour.
At the ninth hour, Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which translated means, “My God, My God, why hast Thou forsaken Me?”
Some of those standing nearby heard and said, “Look, He is calling Elijah.”
Someone ran, filled a sponge with sour wine, placed it on a reed, and gave Him a drink, saying, “Leave Him; let us see whether Elijah comes to take Him down.”
Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed His last.
The curtain of the sanctuary was torn in two from top to bottom.
When the centurion standing opposite Him saw that He breathed His last in this way, he said, “Truly this Man was God’s Son.”
There were also women watching from a distance, among them Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the Little and Joses, and Salome.
When He was in Galilee, they had followed Him and served Him; there were also many other women who had come up with Him to Jerusalem.
Evening had already come, and since it was Preparation—that is, the day before the Sabbath—
Joseph of Arimathea, a respected council member who himself was also awaiting the kingdom of God, came and dared to enter before Pilate and ask for Jesus’ body.
Pilate marveled that He was already dead. Calling the centurion to him, he asked whether He had died some time ago.
When he learned from the centurion, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
Joseph bought a linen cloth, took Him down, wrapped Him in the cloth, and laid Him in a tomb cut out of rock. He rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses watched where He was laid.
When the Sabbath had passed, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might come and anoint Him.
Very early on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb when the sun had risen.
They said to one another, “Who will roll the stone away from the entrance of the tomb for us?”
Looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away, for it was very large.
They entered the tomb and saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were greatly alarmed.
He said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has been raised; He is not here. Look, the place where they laid Him.
But go, tell His disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him, just as He told you.’”
They went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment held them. They said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
⟦After He had risen early on the first day of the week, He appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom He had cast out seven demons.
She went and reported to those who had been with Him, as they mourned and wept.
When they heard that He was alive and had been seen by her, they disbelieved.
After these things, He appeared in another form to two of them as they were walking, going into the country.
They went away and reported to the rest; they did not believe them either.
Later He appeared to the Eleven themselves as they reclined at table, and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart because they had not believed those who had seen Him raised.
He said to them, “Go into the whole world and proclaim the gospel to all creation.
The one who believes and is baptized will be saved; the one who disbelieves will be condemned.
These signs will accompany those who believe: in My name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues;
and with their hands they will pick up snakes; and if they drink anything deadly, it will certainly not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.”
So the Lord Jesus, after speaking to them, was taken up into heaven and sat at the right of God.
They went out and proclaimed everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the accompanying signs.⟧
Since many have undertaken to compile an account of the events fulfilled among us,
just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word handed them down to us,
it seemed good to me also, having followed everything carefully from the beginning, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus,
so that you may know the certainty of the matters in which you have been instructed.
In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. He had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.
Both were righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the Lord’s commandments and ordinances.
They had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.
While he was serving as priest before God in the order of his division,
according to the priesthood’s custom, he was chosen by lot to enter the Lord’s sanctuary and burn incense.
The whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense.
An angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right of the altar of incense.
Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
But the angel said to him, “Do not fear, Zechariah, for your petition has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall name him John.
You will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth,
for he will be great before the Lord. He will certainly drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.
He will turn many of the sons of Israel to the Lord their God.

He himself will go before Him in Elijah’s spirit and power, to turn fathers’ hearts toward children and the disobedient to the understanding of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a people made ready.”
Zechariah said to the angel, “How will I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.”
The angel answered him, “I am Gabriel, who stands before God, and I was sent to speak to you and announce this good news to you.
And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day these things happen, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled at their appointed time.”
The people were waiting for Zechariah and wondering at his delay in the sanctuary.
When he came out, he could not speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the sanctuary. He kept making signs to them and remained mute.
When the days of his service were completed, he went home.
After those days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and she kept herself secluded for five months, saying,
“This is what the Lord has done for me in these days, when He looked upon me to take away my disgrace among people.”
In the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth,
to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of David’s house. The virgin’s name was Mary.
And he entered and said to her, “Rejoice, you who have been favoured! The Lord is with you.”
She was greatly troubled at the saying and considered what sort of greeting this might be.
The angel said to her, “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with God.
And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a Son, and you shall name Him Jesus.
He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David,
and He will reign over Jacob’s house forever, and His kingdom will have no end.”
Mary said to the angel, “How will this be, since I do not know a man?”
The angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and so the holy One to be born will be called Son of God.
And behold, your relative Elizabeth has also conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren,
for no word from God will be powerless.”
Mary said, “Behold, I am the Lord’s servant. May it happen to me according to your word.” Then the angel departed from her.
In those days Mary arose and went in haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah.
She entered Zechariah’s house and greeted Elizabeth.
When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the infant leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.
She cried out with a loud shout and said, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!
And how is it that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
For behold, when the sound of your greeting entered my ears, the infant in my womb leaped with gladness.
And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of the things spoken to her from the Lord.”
Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord,
and my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior,
because He looked upon the lowly condition of His servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed,
because the Mighty One has done great things for me, and holy is His name.
His mercy is for generations and generations upon those who fear Him.
He has performed a mighty deed with His arm; He scattered the proud in the thought of their heart.
He brought rulers down from thrones and raised up the lowly.
He filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty.
He helped Israel His servant, remembering mercy,
as He spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his offspring forever.”
Mary stayed with her about three months and returned to her home.
When Elizabeth’s time to give birth had come, she bore a son.
Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified His mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her.
On the eighth day they came to circumcise the child and were calling him Zechariah after his father’s name.
But his mother answered, “No; he shall be called John.”
They said to her, “No one among your relatives is called by this name.”
They made signs to his father to ask what he wanted the child to be called.
He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And they all wondered.
Immediately his mouth and tongue were opened, and he spoke, blessing God.
Fear came upon all who lived around them, and all these matters were discussed throughout the whole hill country of Judea.
Everyone who heard took these matters to heart, saying, “What then will this child become?” For the Lord’s hand was indeed with him.
His father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying,
“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, because He has visited and accomplished redemption for His people,
and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David His servant,
as He spoke through the mouth of His holy prophets from long ago:
salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us,
to show mercy to our fathers and remember His holy covenant,
the oath He swore to Abraham our father, to grant us
that, rescued from our enemies’ hand, we might serve Him without fear,
in holiness and righteousness before Him all our days.
And you also, child, will be called prophet of the Most High, for you will go before the Lord to prepare His ways,
to give His people knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of their sins,
through the tender mercy of our God, by which the dawn from on high will visit us,
to shine upon those who sit in darkness and death’s shadow, to direct our feet into a way of peace.”
The child grew and became strong in spirit. He remained in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.
In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus for all the inhabited world to be registered.
This first registration took place while Quirinius was governing Syria.
Everyone went to be registered, each to his own city.
Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to David’s city, which is called Bethlehem, because he belonged to David’s house and family,
to be registered with Mary, who was betrothed to him and was pregnant.
While they were there, the time came for her to give birth.
She bore her firstborn Son, wrapped Him in swaddling cloths, and laid Him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the lodging place.
In that same region there were shepherds living in the fields and keeping watch over their flock through the watches of the night.
An angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the Lord’s glory shone around them; they feared with a great fear.
The angel said to them, “Do not fear, for behold, I announce to you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people:
today in David’s city a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord.
This is the sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.”
Suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, praising God and saying,
“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people of His favour.”
When the angels had departed from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, “Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this event that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.”
They came in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in the manger.
When they saw Him, they made known the saying spoken to them about this Child.
Everyone who heard wondered at what the shepherds told them.
But Mary kept all these matters, pondering them in her heart.
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for everything they had heard and seen, just as it had been spoken to them.
When eight days were completed for His circumcision, He was named Jesus, the name given by the angel before He was conceived in the womb.
When the days of their purification according to Moses’ law were completed, they brought Him up to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord,
as it is written in the Lord’s law: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,”
and to give a sacrifice according to what is said in the Lord’s law: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”
And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem named Simeon. This man was righteous and devout, awaiting Israel’s consolation, and the Holy Spirit was upon him.
It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he saw the Lord’s Christ.
He came in the Spirit into the temple. When the parents brought in the Child Jesus to do for Him what was customary under the law,
he received Him into his arms, blessed God, and said,
“Now, Master, Thou art releasing Thy servant in peace according to Thy word,
because my eyes have seen Thy salvation,
which Thou didst prepare in the sight of all peoples:
a light for revelation to the nations and glory for Thy people Israel.”
His father and mother were wondering at what was being said about Him.
Simeon blessed them and said to His mother Mary, “Behold, this One is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign spoken against—
and a sword will pass through your own soul also—so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.”
There was also a prophetess, Anna, daughter of Phanuel, from the tribe of Asher. She was very old. She had lived with her husband for seven years after marrying as a virgin,
and had been a widow until the age of eighty-four. She did not leave the temple, serving with fasts and petitions night and day.
Coming up at that very hour, she gave thanks to God and spoke about Him to everyone awaiting Jerusalem’s redemption.
When they had completed everything according to the Lord’s law, they returned to Galilee, to their own city of Nazareth.
The Child grew and became strong, being filled with wisdom, and God’s grace was upon Him.
His parents went each year to Jerusalem for the Festival of Passover.
When He became twelve years old, they went up according to the festival’s custom.
When the festival days were over and they were returning, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and His parents did not know.
Supposing Him to be in the traveling company, they went a day’s journey and searched for Him among their relatives and acquaintances.
When they did not find Him, they returned to Jerusalem searching for Him.
After three days they found Him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and questioning them.
All who heard Him were astonished at His understanding and answers.
When His parents saw Him, they were overwhelmed. His mother said to Him, “Child, why hast Thou treated us this way? Behold, Thy father and I have been searching for Thee in anguish.”
He said to them, “Why were you searching for Me? Did you not know that I must be in what belongs to My Father?”
But they did not understand the saying He spoke to them.
He went down with them and came to Nazareth, and He remained subject to them. His mother kept all these matters in her heart.
Jesus advanced in wisdom and age, and in favor with God and people.

In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar’s rule, when Pontius Pilate governed Judea, Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Iturea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene,
during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, God’s word came to John, Zechariah’s son, in the wilderness.
He went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins,
as it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: “A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the Lord’s way; make His paths straight.
Every ravine will be filled, and every mountain and hill brought low. The crooked will become straight, and the rough ways smooth roads,
and all flesh will see God’s salvation.”
So he said to the crowds coming out to be baptized by him, “Brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee the coming wrath?
Produce fruits worthy of repentance, and do not begin saying among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as father.’ For I tell you that God can raise up children for Abraham from these stones.
Already the axe also lies at the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire.”
The crowds asked him, “What then should we do?”
He answered them, “Let the one who has two tunics share with the one who has none, and let the one who has food do likewise.”
Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, “Teacher, what should we do?”
He said to them, “Collect nothing beyond what has been appointed for you.”
Soldiers also asked him, “And we, what should we do?” He said to them, “Extort from no one, do not make false accusations, and be content with your pay.”
As the people were waiting expectantly and everyone was considering in their hearts whether John might be the Christ,
John answered them all, “I baptize you with water, but One stronger than I is coming, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.
His winnowing fork is in His hand, to cleanse His threshing floor thoroughly and gather the wheat into His storehouse; but the chaff He will burn with unquenchable fire.”
With many other exhortations also, he announced good news to the people.
But Herod the tetrarch, rebuked by him concerning Herodias, his brother’s wife, and all the evil things Herod had done,
added this also to them all: he shut John up in prison.
When all the people were baptized, and Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened,
and the Holy Spirit descended upon Him in bodily form like a dove. A voice came from heaven: “Thou art My beloved Son; in Thee I have taken delight.”
Jesus Himself was about thirty years old when He began His ministry. He was the son, as was supposed, of Joseph, of Heli,
of Matthat, of Levi, of Melchi, of Jannai, of Joseph,
of Mattathias, of Amos, of Nahum, of Esli, of Naggai,
of Maath, of Mattathias, of Semein, of Josech, of Joda,
of Joanan, of Rhesa, of Zerubbabel, of Shealtiel, of Neri,
of Melchi, of Addi, of Cosam, of Elmadam, of Er,
of Jesus, of Eliezer, of Jorim, of Matthat, of Levi,
of Simeon, of Judah, of Joseph, of Jonam, of Eliakim,
of Melea, of Menna, of Mattatha, of Nathan, of David,
of Jesse, of Obed, of Boaz, of Sala, of Nahshon,
of Amminadab, of Admin, of Arni, of Hezron, of Perez, of Judah,
of Jacob, of Isaac, of Abraham, of Terah, of Nahor,
of Serug, of Reu, of Peleg, of Eber, of Shelah,
of Cainan, of Arphaxad, of Shem, of Noah, of Lamech,
of Methuselah, of Enoch, of Jared, of Mahalalel, of Cainan,
of Enosh, of Seth, of Adam, of God.
Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led in the Spirit in the wilderness
for forty days, being tested by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and when they were completed He was hungry.
The devil said to Him, “If Thou art God’s Son, tell this stone to become bread.”
Jesus answered him, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’”
Taking Him up, the devil showed Him all the kingdoms of the inhabited world in a moment of time.
The devil said to Him, “I will give Thee all this authority and their glory, because it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I wish.
Therefore, if Thou dost bow down before me, it will all be Thine.”
Jesus answered him, “It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve.’”
He brought Him to Jerusalem, placed Him on the temple’s pinnacle, and said to Him, “If Thou art God’s Son, throw Thyself down from here,
for it is written: ‘He will command His angels concerning Thee, to guard Thee,’
and, ‘They will lift Thee upon their hands, lest Thou strike Thy foot against a stone.’”
Jesus answered him, “It has been said: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”
Having completed every test, the devil departed from Him until an opportune time.
Jesus returned in the Spirit’s power into Galilee, and a report about Him spread throughout the whole surrounding region.
He taught in their synagogues, being glorified by everyone.
He came to Nazareth, where He had been brought up, and according to His custom entered the synagogue on the Sabbath day. He stood up to read.
The scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to Him. Unrolling it, He found the place where it was written:

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He anointed Me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to let the crushed go free,
to proclaim the Lord’s year of favor.”
He rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on Him.
He began to say to them, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your ears.”
All bore witness to Him and wondered at the words of grace coming from His mouth. They said, “Is this not Joseph’s son?”
He said to them, “Surely you will tell Me this proverb: ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ ‘Do here in Thy homeland also everything we heard happened in Capernaum.’”
He said, “Amen, I tell you, no prophet is acceptable in his homeland.
But in truth I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in Elijah’s days, when heaven was shut for three years and six months and a great famine came over the whole land.
Yet Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at Zarephath in Sidon’s territory.
And there were many leprous people in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet, but none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.”
Everyone in the synagogue was filled with anger when they heard these things.
They rose, threw Him out of the city, and led Him to the brow of the hill on which their city was built, intending to hurl Him down.
But He passed through their midst and went on His way.
He went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and was teaching them on the Sabbaths.
They were overwhelmed at His teaching, because His word was with authority.
In the synagogue was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon. He cried out with a loud voice,
“Ah! What have we to do with Thee, Jesus of Nazareth? Hast Thou come to destroy us? I know who Thou art: God’s Holy One.”
Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent and come out of him!” The demon threw him down in their midst and came out of him without harming him.
Amazement came upon everyone, and they said to one another, “What is this word? With authority and power He commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!”
A report about Him went out into every place in the surrounding region.
Leaving the synagogue, He entered Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was gripped by a high fever, and they asked Him about her.
Standing over her, He rebuked the fever, and it left her. Immediately she rose and served them.
As the sun was setting, everyone who had people sick with various diseases brought them to Him. He laid His hands on each one and healed them.
Demons also came out of many, crying, “Thou art God’s Son!” He rebuked them and would not let them speak, because they knew He was the Christ.
When day came, He went out to a deserted place. The crowds searched for Him, came to Him, and tried to keep Him from departing from them.
But He said to them, “I must announce the good news of God’s kingdom to the other cities also, because for this I was sent.”
And He continued proclaiming in the synagogues of Judea.
As the crowd pressed upon Him to hear God’s word, He was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret.
He saw two boats beside the lake; the fishermen had left them and were washing their nets.
He entered one of the boats, which belonged to Simon, and asked him to put out a little from the land. Sitting down, He taught the crowds from the boat.
When He finished speaking, He said to Simon, “Put out into the deep water, and let down your nets for a catch.”
Simon answered, “Master, we labored through the whole night and caught nothing, but at Thy word I will let down the nets.”
When they did this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish, and their nets began to tear.
They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. They came and filled both boats, so that they began to sink.
When Simon Peter saw it, he fell at Jesus’ knees, saying, “Depart from me, Lord, because I am a sinful man.”
For amazement had seized him and everyone with him at the catch of fish they had taken,
and likewise James and John, Zebedee’s sons, who were Simon’s partners. Jesus said to Simon, “Do not fear. From now on you will be catching people alive.”
They brought the boats to land, left everything, and followed Him.
While He was in one of the cities, behold, there was a man full of leprosy. Seeing Jesus, he fell on his face and petitioned Him, saying, “Lord, if Thou art willing, Thou canst cleanse me.”
Stretching out His hand, He touched him and said, “I am willing; be cleansed.” Immediately the leprosy departed from him.
He commanded him to tell no one: “But go, show yourself to the priest, and make the offering for your cleansing as Moses commanded, for a testimony to them.”
Yet the report about Him spread all the more, and large crowds gathered to hear and to be healed of their illnesses.
But He kept withdrawing to deserted places and praying.

On one of those days He was teaching, and Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there. They had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem; and the Lord’s power was present for Him to heal.
And behold, men were carrying on a bed a man who was paralyzed. They sought to bring him in and place him before Him.
Finding no way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof and lowered him through the tiles with his little bed into their midst, before Jesus.
Seeing their faith, He said, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.”
The scribes and Pharisees began to reason, saying, “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins except God alone?”
Jesus recognized their thoughts and answered them, “What are you reasoning in your hearts?
Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’?
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—He said to the paralyzed man—“I tell you, rise, take up your little bed, and go home.”
Immediately he rose before them, took up what he had been lying on, and went home glorifying God.
Astonishment seized everyone, and they glorified God and were filled with fear, saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.”
After this He went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth, and said to him, “Follow Me.”
Leaving everything, he rose and followed Him.
Levi gave a great reception for Him in his house. A large crowd of tax collectors and others was reclining with them.
The Pharisees and their scribes grumbled to His disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”
Jesus answered them, “Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do.
I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
They said to Him, “John’s disciples fast often and offer petitions, and likewise those of the Pharisees, but Thine eat and drink.”
Jesus said to them, “Can you make the bridegroom’s companions fast while the bridegroom is with them?
But days will come, and when the bridegroom is taken from them, then they will fast in those days.”
He also told them a parable: “No one tears a patch from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. Otherwise he will tear the new one, and the patch from the new will not match the old.
And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise the new wine will burst the skins, and it will be poured out and the skins destroyed.
But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.
And no one who has drunk old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’”
On a Sabbath He was passing through grainfields. His disciples plucked the ears, rubbed them in their hands, and ate.
Some of the Pharisees said, “Why are you doing what is not lawful on the Sabbaths?”
Jesus answered them, “Have you not even read what David did when he and those with him were hungry,
how he entered God’s house, took and ate the loaves of the presentation, and gave them to those with him, although no one except the priests alone may lawfully eat them?”
He said to them, “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”
On another Sabbath He entered the synagogue and taught. A man was there whose right hand was withered.
The scribes and Pharisees watched closely to see whether He would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a way to accuse Him.
But He knew their thoughts and said to the man with the withered hand, “Rise and stand in the middle.” He rose and stood.
Jesus said to them, “I ask you: Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or do evil, to save a life or destroy it?”
Looking around at all of them, He said to him, “Stretch out your hand.” He did so, and his hand was restored.
They were filled with mindless anger and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.
In those days He went out to the mountain to pray, and spent the night in prayer to God.
When day came, He called His disciples and chose twelve from them, whom He also named apostles:
Simon, whom He also named Peter, and his brother Andrew, and James and John, and Philip and Bartholomew,
and Matthew and Thomas, and James son of Alphaeus, and Simon called the Zealot,
and Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
He came down with them and stood on a level place. There was a large crowd of His disciples and a great multitude of the people from all Judea, Jerusalem, and the coastal region of Tyre and Sidon.
They had come to hear Him and be healed of their diseases; those troubled by unclean spirits were also healed.
The whole crowd sought to touch Him, because power went out from Him and healed everyone.
Lifting His eyes toward His disciples, He said, “Blessed are you who are poor, because yours is God’s kingdom.
Blessed are you who hunger now, because you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, because you will laugh.
Blessed are you when people hate you, when they exclude you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil because of the Son of Man.
Rejoice on that day and leap, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; their fathers treated the prophets in the same way.
But woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation.
Woe to you who are filled now, because you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, because you will mourn and weep.
Woe when all people speak well of you, for their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way.
But I say to you who hear: Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you.
Bless those who curse you; pray for those who mistreat you.
Offer the other cheek also to the one striking you on the cheek; and from the one taking your cloak, do not withhold your tunic also.
Give to everyone who asks you, and do not demand back your belongings from the one who takes them.
As you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them.
If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.
If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners do the same.
If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners to receive the equivalent back.
But love your enemies, do good, and lend, expecting nothing back. Your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, because He is kind to the ungrateful and evil.
Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.
Do not judge, and you will certainly not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will certainly not be condemned. Release, and you will be released.
Give, and it will be given to you. They will put into your lap a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, overflowing; for by the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you.”
He also told them a parable: “Can a blind person guide a blind person? Will they not both fall into a pit?
A disciple is not above the teacher, but everyone fully trained will be like his teacher.
Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?

How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite! First take the beam out of your eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye.
For no good tree produces rotten fruit, nor again does a rotten tree produce good fruit.
Each tree is known by its own fruit. People do not gather figs from thorns, nor harvest grapes from a bramble.
The good person brings out good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil person brings out evil from the evil treasure; for his mouth speaks from the heart’s abundance.
Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?
Everyone who comes to Me, hears My words and does them—I will show you whom he resembles.

He resembles a man building a house, who dug and went deep and laid a foundation on the rock. When a flood came, the river burst against that house but could not shake it, because it had been well built.

But the one who heard and did not act resembles a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. The river burst against it, and immediately it collapsed; the ruin of that house was great.”
When He had finished all His sayings in the people’s hearing, He entered Capernaum.
A certain centurion had a slave who was ill and about to die, and who was precious to him.
Hearing about Jesus, he sent elders of the Jews to Him, asking Him to come and save his slave.
When they reached Jesus, they urged Him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy for Thee to grant him this,
for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue for us.”
Jesus went with them. When He was already not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to Him, “Lord, do not trouble Thyself, for I am not worthy for Thee to enter under my roof.
Therefore I did not even consider myself worthy to come to Thee. But speak a word, and let my servant be healed.
For I too am a man placed under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and my slave, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”
When Jesus heard this, He marveled at him. Turning to the crowd following Him, He said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”
Those who had been sent returned to the house and found the slave in good health.
Afterward He went to a city called Nain, and His disciples and a large crowd traveled with Him.
As He approached the city’s gate, behold, a dead man was being carried out, his mother’s only son. She was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the city was with her.
When the Lord saw her, He was moved with compassion for her and said, “Do not weep.”
He approached and touched the bier; the bearers stood still. He said, “Young man, I tell you, rise.”
The dead man sat up and began speaking, and He gave him to his mother.
Fear seized everyone, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us,” and, “God has visited His people.”
This report about Him spread throughout all Judea and all the surrounding region.
John’s disciples reported all these things to him. John called two of his disciples
and sent them to the Lord, saying, “Art Thou the One who is coming, or should we expect another?”
When the men came to Him, they said, “John the Baptist sent us to Thee, saying, ‘Art Thou the One who is coming, or should we expect another?’”
At that hour He healed many of diseases, afflictions and evil spirits, and graciously gave sight to many blind people.

He answered them, “Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind recover sight, the lame walk, leprous people are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor receive good news.
And blessed is whoever does not stumble because of Me.”
When John’s messengers had departed, He began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to behold? A reed shaken by the wind?
But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who live in splendid clothing and luxury are in royal palaces.
But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send My messenger before Thy face, who will prepare Thy way ahead of Thee.’
I tell you, among those born of women no one is greater than John; yet the lesser one in God’s kingdom is greater than he.”
When all the people and the tax collectors heard, they acknowledged God’s righteousness, having been baptized with John’s baptism.
But the Pharisees and experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for themselves, not having been baptized by him.
“To what, then, shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like?
They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, saying, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not weep.’
For John the Baptist has come neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’
The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Behold, a glutton and wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.’
Yet wisdom was justified by all her children.”
One of the Pharisees asked Him to eat with him. He entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined at table.
And behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner learned that He was reclining in the Pharisee’s house. She brought an alabaster vessel of perfume
and stood behind Him at His feet, weeping. She began to wet His feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head. She kept kissing His feet and anointing them with the perfume.
When the Pharisee who had invited Him saw it, he said within himself, “If this man were a prophet, He would know who and what sort of woman is touching Him, that she is a sinner.”
Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to say to you.” He said, “Teacher, say it.”
“A certain lender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty.
Since they had nothing with which to repay, he graciously forgave them both. Which of them, then, will love him more?”
Simon answered, “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more.” He said to him, “You judged correctly.”
Turning toward the woman, He said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave Me no water for My feet, but she wet My feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.
You gave Me no kiss, but from the time I entered she has not stopped kissing My feet.
You did not anoint My head with oil, but she anointed My feet with perfume.
For this reason I tell you: her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much. But the one who is forgiven little loves little.”
He said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.”
Those reclining with Him began to say within themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?”
And He said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
After this He traveled through cities and villages, proclaiming and announcing the good news of God’s kingdom. The Twelve were with Him,
and certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and illnesses: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out,
Joanna, wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward, Susanna, and many others, who served them out of their own belongings.
When a large crowd was gathering and people from each city were coming to Him, He spoke through a parable:
“The sower went out to sow his seed. As he sowed, some fell beside the road, was trampled, and the birds of the sky ate it.
Other seed fell on the rock, and when it sprouted it withered because it had no moisture.
Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it.
Other seed fell into good soil, sprouted and produced fruit a hundredfold.” As He said these things, He called out, “Let the one who has ears to hear listen.”
His disciples asked Him what this parable meant.
He said, “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of God’s kingdom, but to the rest in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.
This is the parable: the seed is God’s word.
Those beside the road are the ones who have heard; then the devil comes and takes the word from their heart, so that they may not believe and be saved.
Those on the rock are the ones who, when they hear, receive the word with joy. They have no root; they believe for a time and fall away in a time of testing.
What fell among thorns represents those who have heard, but as they go along they are choked by life’s cares, wealth and pleasures, and do not bring fruit to maturity.
What is in the good soil represents those who hear the word in a noble and good heart, hold it fast, and bear fruit with endurance.
No one lights a lamp and covers it with a vessel or puts it under a bed, but places it on a lampstand, so that those entering may see the light.
For nothing is hidden that will not become manifest, nor concealed that will not be known and come into the open.
Therefore watch how you hear. For whoever has will be given more, and whoever does not have will have even what he thinks he has taken from him.”
His mother and brothers came to Him but could not reach Him because of the crowd.
It was reported to Him, “Thy mother and Thy brothers are standing outside, wanting to see Thee.”
He answered them, “My mother and My brothers are these who hear God’s word and do it.”
On one of those days He entered a boat with His disciples and said to them, “Let us cross to the other side of the lake.” They put out.
As they sailed, He fell asleep. A windstorm came down upon the lake, and they were being swamped and were in danger.
They came and woke Him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” He awoke and rebuked the wind and the surging water. They ceased, and there was calm.
He said to them, “Where is your faith?” Afraid, they marveled and said to one another, “Who then is this, that He commands even the winds and the water, and they obey Him?”
They sailed into the country of the Gerasenes, which lies opposite Galilee.
When He stepped onto the land, a man from the city who had demons met Him. For a considerable time he had worn no garment and had not lived in a house, but among the tombs.
Seeing Jesus, he cried out, fell before Him, and said with a loud voice, “What have I to do with Thee, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg Thee, do not torment me!”

For He was commanding the unclean spirit to leave the man. It had seized him many times; he was bound with chains and shackles and kept under guard, but he broke the bonds and was driven by the demon into deserted places.
Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He said, “Legion,” because many demons had entered him.
They begged Him not to command them to go away into the abyss.
A herd of many pigs was feeding there on the hillside. They begged Him to permit them to enter those pigs, and He permitted them.
The demons came out of the man and entered the pigs. The herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and was drowned.
When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and reported it in the city and in the fields.
People came out to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone out sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid.
Those who had seen reported to them how the demon-possessed man had been saved.
The whole multitude of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked Him to depart from them, because they were gripped by great fear. He entered a boat and returned.
The man from whom the demons had gone out begged to be with Him, but He sent him away, saying,
“Return to your home and recount everything God has done for you.” He went away proclaiming throughout the whole city everything Jesus had done for him.
When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed Him, for they were all awaiting Him.
And behold, a man named Jairus came, who was a ruler of the synagogue. Falling at Jesus’ feet, he begged Him to enter his house,
because he had an only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying. As He went, the crowds pressed closely around Him.
A woman had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years. She had spent her whole livelihood on physicians, but could not be healed by anyone.
Coming up behind Him, she touched the fringe of His garment, and immediately her flow of blood stopped.
Jesus said, “Who touched Me?” When everyone denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds surround Thee and press against Thee.”
Jesus said, “Someone touched Me, for I knew that power had gone out from Me.”
When the woman saw that she had not escaped notice, she came trembling and fell before Him. Before all the people she reported why she had touched Him and how she had been healed immediately.
He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
While He was still speaking, someone came from the synagogue ruler’s house, saying, “Your daughter has died. Do not trouble the Teacher any longer.”
Jesus heard and answered him, “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be saved.”
When He came to the house, He allowed no one to enter with Him except Peter, John and James, and the child’s father and mother.
Everyone was weeping and beating themselves in mourning for her. He said, “Do not weep, for she has not died, but is sleeping.”
They laughed at Him, knowing that she had died.
But He took her hand and called, “Child, rise.”
Her spirit returned, and she rose immediately. He ordered that she be given something to eat.
Her parents were astonished, but He commanded them to tell no one what had happened.
Calling the Twelve together, He gave them power and authority over all demons and to heal diseases.
He sent them to proclaim God’s kingdom and heal the sick.
He said to them, “Take nothing for the journey: neither a staff nor a bag nor bread nor silver; neither are you to have two tunics each.
Whatever house you enter, remain there and depart from there.
Wherever people do not receive you, as you leave that city shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.”
They went out and passed through the villages, announcing good news and healing everywhere.
Herod the tetrarch heard of everything that was happening and was perplexed, because some were saying that John had been raised from the dead,
others that Elijah had appeared, and others that one of the ancient prophets had arisen.
Herod said, “John I beheaded. But who is this about whom I hear such things?” And he sought to see Him.
When the apostles returned, they recounted to Him everything they had done. Taking them with Him, He withdrew privately to a city called Bethsaida.
The crowds learned of it and followed Him. He welcomed them, spoke to them about God’s kingdom, and healed those needing a cure.

The day was beginning to draw to a close. The Twelve approached and said to Him, “Dismiss the crowd, so that they may go into the surrounding villages and countryside, find lodging and obtain provisions, because we are here in a deserted place.”
He said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish, unless we ourselves go and buy food for all these people.”
For there were about five thousand men. He said to His disciples, “Have them recline in groups of about fifty each.”
They did so and had everyone recline.
Taking the five loaves and the two fish, He looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, and kept giving them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
They all ate and were filled, and the leftover fragments were gathered up: twelve baskets.
While He was praying apart, His disciples were with Him, and He asked them, “Who do the crowds say I am?”
They answered, “John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and others that one of the ancient prophets has arisen.”
He said to them, “But you, who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “God’s Christ.”
He sternly commanded them to tell this to no one,
saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and on the third day be raised.”
He said to everyone, “If anyone wishes to come after Me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow Me.
For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will save it.
For what benefit is there for a person to gain the whole world but destroy or forfeit himself?
Whoever is ashamed of Me and My words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when He comes in His glory and that of the Father and the holy angels.
But truly I tell you, some standing here will certainly not taste death until they see God’s kingdom.”
About eight days after these sayings, He took Peter, John and James and went up the mountain to pray.
As He prayed, the appearance of His face became different, and His clothing became white and flashing like lightning.
And behold, two men were speaking with Him, who were Moses and Elijah.
Appearing in glory, they spoke of His departure, which He was about to fulfill in Jerusalem.
Peter and those with him were weighed down with sleep, but when fully awake they saw His glory and the two men standing with Him.
As they were parting from Him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good for us to be here. Let us make three tents, one for Thee, one for Moses and one for Elijah,” not knowing what he was saying.
While he said this, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud.
A voice came from the cloud, saying, “This is My Son, the chosen One; listen to Him.”
When the voice came, Jesus was found alone. They kept silent and in those days reported to no one anything they had seen.
On the following day, when they came down from the mountain, a large crowd met Him.
And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, “Teacher, I beg Thee to look upon my son, because he is my only child.
Behold, a spirit seizes him, and suddenly he cries out. It convulses him with foaming and scarcely leaves him, bruising him.
I begged Thy disciples to cast it out, but they could not.”
Jesus answered, “O faithless and distorted generation, how long shall I be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.”
While he was still approaching, the demon dashed him down and convulsed him. Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.
Everyone was overwhelmed at God’s majesty. While they all marveled at everything He was doing, He said to His disciples,
“You, place these words in your ears: the Son of Man is about to be handed over into human hands.”
But they did not understand this saying; it was veiled from them so that they might not perceive it, and they were afraid to ask Him about it.
A discussion arose among them about which of them might be greatest.
Jesus knew the thought of their heart. He took a child and placed him beside Himself,
and said to them, “Whoever receives this child in My name receives Me; whoever receives Me receives the One who sent Me. For the one who is least among you all is great.”
John answered, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in Thy name and tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.”
Jesus said to him, “Do not stop him, for whoever is not against you is for you.”
As the days for His being taken up approached their fulfillment, He firmly set His face to go to Jerusalem.
He sent messengers before His face. They went and entered a Samaritan village to prepare for Him.
But they did not receive Him, because His face was set toward Jerusalem.
Seeing this, the disciples James and John said, “Lord, dost Thou wish us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?”
But He turned and rebuked them.
And they went to another village.
As they traveled on the road, someone said to Him, “I will follow Thee wherever Thou goest.”
Jesus said to him, “Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have dwelling places, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head.”
He said to another, “Follow Me.” But he said, “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.”
He said to him, “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you go and proclaim God’s kingdom.”
Another also said, “I will follow Thee, Lord; but first permit me to say farewell to those in my house.”
Jesus said to him, “No one who puts his hand to a plow and looks backward is fit for God’s kingdom.”
After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others also, and sent them two by two before His face into every city and place where He Himself was about to go.
He said to them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Therefore petition the Lord of the harvest to send workers out into His harvest.
Go; behold, I send you as lambs among wolves.
Carry no purse, no bag, no sandals, and greet no one along the road.
Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house.’
If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; otherwise it will return to you.
Remain in that same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the worker is worthy of his pay. Do not move from house to house.
Whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat what is set before you.
Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘God’s kingdom has drawn near to you.’
But whatever city you enter and they do not receive you, go out into its streets and say,
‘Even the dust from your city that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this: God’s kingdom has drawn near.’
I tell you, it will be more bearable for Sodom on that day than for that city.
Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty deeds performed among you had happened in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.
Nevertheless, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgment than for you.
And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted as far as heaven? You will go down as far as Hades.
The one who hears you hears Me, and the one who rejects you rejects Me; the one who rejects Me rejects the One who sent Me.”
The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons submit to us in Thy name.”
He said to them, “I was watching Satan fall from heaven like lightning.
Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions, and over all the enemy’s power, and nothing will ever harm you.
Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names have been written in the heavens.”

At that very hour He rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I acknowledge Thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because Thou didst hide these things from the wise and understanding and reveal them to infants. Yes, Father, for such was Thy good pleasure.
Everything has been handed over to Me by My Father. No one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him.”
Turning privately to the disciples, He said, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.
For I tell you that many prophets and kings wished to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.”
And behold, an expert in the law stood up to test Him, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
He said to him, “What is written in the law? How do you read it?”
He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God from your whole heart, with your whole soul, with your whole strength and with your whole mind, and your neighbor as yourself.”
He said to him, “You answered correctly. Do this and you will live.”
But wishing to justify himself, he said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?”
