From one He made every nation of humanity to live upon the whole face of the earth, determining their appointed times and the boundaries of their dwelling,
so that they might seek God, if perhaps they might feel their way toward Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us.
For in Him we live and move and exist, as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we too are His offspring.’
Since we are God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine nature is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by human art and thought.
Therefore, having overlooked the times of ignorance, God now commands all people everywhere to repent,
because He has fixed a day on which He will judge the inhabited world in righteousness through a Man whom He appointed, giving assurance to everyone by raising Him from the dead.”
When they heard of a resurrection of the dead, some mocked, while others said, “We will hear you again about this.”
So Paul went out from their midst.
But some people joined him and believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
After these things he left Athens and came to Corinth.
He found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to them,
and because he practiced the same trade, he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.
Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue and sought to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself to the word, bearing solemn witness to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.
When they opposed him and spoke abusively, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be upon your own heads. I am clean. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”
He left there and entered the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God, whose house was next to the synagogue.
Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believed in the Lord with his whole household. Many of the Corinthians who heard believed and were baptized.
The Lord said to Paul by a vision in the night, “Do not fear, but speak and do not be silent,
because I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.”
He stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
While Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews rose together against Paul and brought him before the tribunal,
saying, “This man persuades people to worship God contrary to the law.”
As Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were some wrongdoing or wicked crime, O Jews, I would have reason to hear you out.
But if these are questions about a word, names, and your own law, see to it yourselves. I do not wish to be a judge of these things.”
He drove them away from the tribunal.
They all seized Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler, and beat him before the tribunal. Gallio cared about none of these things.
Paul stayed many more days, then took leave of the brothers and sailed for Syria, with Priscilla and Aquila. He had cut his hair at Cenchreae, for he had a vow.
They arrived at Ephesus, and he left them there. He himself entered the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay for a longer time, he did not agree.
Instead, he took leave of them, saying, “I will return to you again, God willing,” and sailed from Ephesus.
He landed at Caesarea, went up and greeted the Church, and went down to Antioch.
After spending some time there, he departed and traveled from place to place through the Galatian region and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
A Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, powerful in the Scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only John’s baptism.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.
When he wished to cross over to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. On arriving, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace,
for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, demonstrating through the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.
While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul passed through the upper regions and came down to Ephesus. He found some disciples
and said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They said to him, “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.”
He said, “Into what, then, were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.”
Paul said, “John baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the One coming after him, that is, in Jesus.”
When they heard this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
When Paul laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.
There were about twelve men in all.
He entered the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, reasoning and persuading concerning the kingdom of God.

But when some became hardened and refused to believe, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude, he withdrew from them and separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
This continued for two years, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.
God was doing extraordinary mighty works through Paul’s hands,
so that even cloths or aprons from contact with his skin were carried to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits went out.
Some itinerant Jewish exorcists also attempted to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I solemnly charge you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.”
Seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this.
But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?”
The man in whom the evil spirit was leaped upon them, mastered both of them, and overpowered them, so that they fled from that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus. Fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
Many who had believed came, confessing and reporting their practices.
A considerable number who had practiced magic brought their books together and burned them before everyone. They calculated their prices and found the total to be fifty thousand in silver.
In this way the word of the Lord grew mightily and prevailed.
After these things were completed, Paul resolved in spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”
He sent two of those who assisted him, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself remained in Asia for a time.
About that time a serious disturbance arose concerning the Way.
A silversmith named Demetrius, who made silver shrines of Artemis, provided considerable business for the craftsmen.
He gathered them and the workers in related trades and said, “Men, you know that our prosperity comes from this business.
You see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a considerable crowd, saying that things made by hands are not gods.

There is danger not only that this trade of ours will fall into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be reckoned as nothing, and that she whom all Asia and the inhabited world worship will be stripped of her magnificence.”
When they heard this, they became full of rage and cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The city was filled with confusion. They rushed together into the theater, seizing Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who traveled with Paul.
Paul wanted to enter among the populace, but the disciples would not let him.
Even some of the Asiarchs, who were his friends, sent to him and urged him not to venture into the theater.
Some shouted one thing and some another, for the assembly was confused, and most did not know why they had come together.
They prompted Alexander from the crowd, the Jews having put him forward. Alexander motioned with his hand and wished to make a defense before the populace.
When they recognized that he was a Jew, one cry arose from them all for about two hours: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The city secretary quieted the crowd and said, “Men of Ephesus, who among human beings does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple-keeper of the great Artemis and of what fell from Zeus?
Since these things are undeniable, you must remain calm and do nothing rash.
For you have brought these men here, though they are neither temple-robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
If Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a charge against anyone, court sessions are held and proconsuls are available; let them bring charges against one another.
But if you seek anything further, it will be settled in the lawful assembly.
For we are in danger of being charged with rioting over today’s events, since there is no cause for it; we will not be able to give an account of this gathering.”
After saying these things, he dismissed the assembly.
After the uproar ceased, Paul summoned the disciples and encouraged them. Taking leave of them, he departed for Macedonia.
He passed through those regions and encouraged them with many words, then came to Greece
and spent three months there. When a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.
He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea; Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica; Gaius from Derbe, and Timothy; and Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia.
These men went ahead and waited for us in Troas.
We sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and came to them at Troas in five days, where we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread, Paul spoke with them. He intended to leave the next day and prolonged his message until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upper room where we had gathered.
A young man named Eutychus sat in the window and was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul continued speaking at length. Overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was picked up dead.
Paul went down, fell upon him, embraced him, and said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.”
He went back up, broke the bread and ate, and talked for a long time until dawn. Then he departed.
They brought the boy away alive and were greatly comforted.
We went ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for he had arranged it this way, intending himself to travel on foot.
When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene.
Sailing from there, the next day we arrived opposite Chios; on the following day we put in at Samos, and on the next we came to Miletus.
For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so that he would not spend time in Asia. He was hurrying, if possible, to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the Church.
When they came to him, he said, “You know how I was with you the whole time, from the first day I set foot in Asia,
serving the Lord with all humility, tears, and trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews.
I did not hold back from declaring anything beneficial to you and teaching you publicly and from house to house,
bearing solemn witness to both Jews and Greeks of repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus.
And now, look, bound in spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will meet me there,
except that in every city the Holy Spirit bears witness to me, saying that bonds and afflictions await me.
But I consider my life of no value to myself, so that I may complete my course and the ministry I received from the Lord Jesus: to bear solemn witness to the good news of God’s grace.
And now, look, I know that none of you among whom I went about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again.
Therefore I testify to you this very day that I am clean from the blood of all,
for I did not hold back from declaring to you the whole purpose of God.
Pay attention to yourselves and to all the flock, among whom the Holy Spirit has placed you as overseers, to shepherd the Church of God, which He acquired through His own blood.
I know that after my departure fierce wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock.
Even from among you yourselves men will arise, speaking distorted things to draw the disciples away after themselves.
Therefore stay awake, remembering that for three years, night and day, I never ceased admonishing each one with tears.
And now I entrust you to God and to the word of His grace, which is able to build you up and give you the inheritance among all who have been sanctified.
I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands served my needs and those of the people with me.
In everything I showed you that by working in this way we must support the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that He Himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”
After saying these things, he knelt down with them all and prayed.
They all wept greatly, threw their arms around Paul’s neck, and kissed him repeatedly,
grieving most of all over the word he had spoken, that they would no longer see his face. They accompanied him to the ship.
When we had torn ourselves away from them and set sail, we made a straight course to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
We found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, went aboard, and set sail.
We sighted Cyprus and passed it on our left, sailed toward Syria, and landed at Tyre, for the ship was to unload its cargo there.
We sought out the disciples and stayed there seven days. Through the Spirit they told Paul not to set foot in Jerusalem.
When our days there were completed, we left and went on our way. They all accompanied us, with wives and children, as far as outside the city. We knelt on the beach and prayed,
then said farewell to one another. We boarded the ship, and they returned to their homes.
Completing the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, greeted the brothers, and stayed with them for one day.
The next day we departed and came to Caesarea. We entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
He had four daughters who were virgins and prophesied.
While we stayed for several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘The Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man whose belt this is in this way and hand him over into Gentile hands.’”
When we heard these things, both we and the local people urged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
Since he would not be persuaded, we became silent and said, “Let the Lord’s will be done.”
After these days we made our preparations and went up to Jerusalem.
Some disciples from Caesarea also went with us, taking us to a certain Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we were to lodge.
When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us gladly.
The next day Paul went with us to James, and all the elders were present.
After greeting them, he related one by one the things God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
When they heard, they glorified God and said to him, “You see, brother, how many tens of thousands of Jews have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.
They have been informed about you that you teach all the Jews among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk in the customs.
What, then, is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.
Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow upon themselves.

Take these men, purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that there is nothing to what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also walk in step, keeping the law.
But concerning the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent word, judging that they should keep themselves from what is sacrificed to idols, blood, what is strangled, and sexual immorality.”

Then Paul took the men, and on the next day, after purifying himself with them, he entered the temple, giving notice of the completion of the days of purification, up to the presentation of the offering for each one of them.
When the seven days were about to be completed, the Jews from Asia saw him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd, and laid hands on him,

crying, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people, the law, and this place. Moreover, he has even brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place.”
For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city and supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him outside the temple, and immediately the doors were shut.
While they were seeking to kill him, a report reached the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion.
He immediately took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. When they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Then the tribune approached, seized him, and ordered him bound with two chains. He asked who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd shouted one thing and some another. Since he could learn nothing certain because of the uproar, he ordered Paul to be brought into the barracks.
When he reached the steps, the soldiers had to carry him because of the crowd’s violence,
for the multitude of the people followed, crying, “Away with him!”
As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, “May I say something to you?” He said, “Do you know Greek?
Then are you not the Egyptian who some time ago stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Sicarii into the wilderness?”
Paul said, “I am a Jewish man from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I ask you, allow me to speak to the people.”
When he gave permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned with his hand to the people. When a great silence fell, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:
“Men, brothers and fathers, hear the defense I now make before you.”
When they heard that he addressed them in the Hebrew language, they became still quieter. He said:
“I am a Jewish man, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, educated in the strict observance of the ancestral law, zealous for God as all of you are today.
I persecuted this Way to the point of death, binding and handing over to prisons both men and women,

as the high priest and the whole council of elders can testify for me. From them I also received letters to the brothers, and I went toward Damascus to bring those there bound to Jerusalem for punishment.
As I was traveling and drawing near Damascus, about noon, a brilliant light from heaven suddenly flashed around me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?’
I answered, ‘Who art Thou, Lord?’ He said to me, ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.’
Those with me saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the One speaking to me.
I said, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ The Lord said to me, ‘Rise and go into Damascus, and there you will be told about everything appointed for you to do.’
Since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those with me and came into Damascus.
A certain Ananias, a man devout according to the law and well spoken of by all the Jews living there,
came to me, stood beside me, and said, ‘Brother Saul, regain your sight.’ At that very hour I regained my sight and looked at him.
He said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know His will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from His mouth,
for you will be His witness to all people of what you have seen and heard.
Now why do you delay? Rise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling upon His name.’
After I returned to Jerusalem, while I was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance
and saw Him saying to me, ‘Hurry, and go out quickly from Jerusalem, because they will not accept your testimony about Me.’
I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that I used to imprison and beat in the synagogues those who believe in Thee.
And when the blood of Stephen, Thy witness, was being poured out, I myself stood by, approving and guarding the garments of those who were killing him.’
He said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’”
They listened to him until this statement, then raised their voice and said, “Remove such a man from the earth, for he ought not to live.”
As they shouted, flung their garments, and threw dust into the air,
the tribune ordered him brought into the barracks and directed that he be examined by scourging, so that he might learn why they were shouting against him in this way.
As they stretched him out with the straps, Paul said to the centurion standing nearby, “Is it lawful for you to scourge a Roman citizen who has not been condemned?”
When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and reported it, saying, “What are you about to do? This man is a Roman.”
The tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman?” He said, “Yes.”
The tribune answered, “I acquired this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said, “But I was born with it.”
Those about to examine him immediately withdrew. The tribune too was afraid when he learned that Paul was a Roman and that he had bound him.

The next day, wishing to learn with certainty what accusation the Jews were bringing against him, he unbound him and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to assemble. He brought Paul down and set him before them.
Paul looked intently at the council and said, “Men, brothers, I have conducted my life before God with an entirely good conscience to this day.”
The high priest Ananias ordered those standing beside him to strike his mouth.
Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, whitewashed wall! You sit judging me according to the law, yet in violation of the law you order me struck?”
Those standing nearby said, “Are you insulting God’s high priest?”
Paul said, “Brothers, I did not know that he was high priest, for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’”

When Paul perceived that one part consisted of Sadducees and the other of Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Men, brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. I am being judged concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead.”
As he said this, dissension arose between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the multitude was divided.
For the Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor angel nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge both.
A great outcry arose, and some scribes of the Pharisees’ party stood up and argued fiercely, saying, “We find nothing wrong in this man. But what if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?”
As the dispute intensified, the tribune feared Paul would be torn apart by them. He ordered the troops to go down, snatch him from their midst, and bring him into the barracks.
The following night the Lord stood beside him and said, “Take courage, for as you have borne solemn witness about Me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome.”
When day came, the Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves under a curse, saying they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
More than forty had made this conspiracy.
They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have bound ourselves under a solemn curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.
Now, therefore, you and the council should inform the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you intended to determine his case more accurately. We are ready to kill him before he comes near.”
Paul’s sister’s son heard about the ambush, came and entered the barracks, and reported it to Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to report to him.”
So he took him and brought him to the tribune, saying, “The prisoner Paul called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, since he has something to tell you.”
The tribune took him by the hand, withdrew privately, and asked, “What is it that you have to report to me?”
He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though it intended to inquire more accurately about him.

But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty men among them are lying in wait for him. They have bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they kill him, and now they are ready, awaiting your agreement.”
The tribune dismissed the young man, ordering him, “Tell no one that you have disclosed these things to me.”
He called two of the centurions and said, “Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, leaving at the third hour of the night.”
He also ordered mounts to be provided so that they could put Paul on them and bring him safely to Felix the governor.
He wrote a letter in this form:
“Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix: greetings.
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came with the troops and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman.
Wishing to learn the reason they accused him, I brought him down to their council.
I found him accused over questions of their law, but under no charge deserving death or imprisonment.
When a plot against the man was disclosed to me, I immediately sent him to you, also ordering his accusers to state their case against him before you.”
So the soldiers, according to their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.
The next day they left the horsemen to go on with him and returned to the barracks.
When the horsemen entered Caesarea, they delivered the letter to the governor and also presented Paul before him.
He read it, asked what province Paul was from, and learned that he was from Cilicia.
He said, “I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive,” and ordered him kept under guard in Herod’s praetorium.
After five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and an advocate named Tertullus. They presented their case against Paul to the governor.
When Paul was called, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying, “Through you we enjoy much peace, and reforms are being made for this nation through your foresight.
In every way and everywhere we acknowledge this, most excellent Felix, with all gratitude.
But so that I may not detain you further, I ask you in your kindness to hear us briefly.
For we have found this man to be a plague, stirring up disturbances among all the Jews throughout the inhabited world, and a ringleader of the party of the Nazarenes.
He even tried to profane the temple, and we seized him.
By examining him yourself, you will be able to learn about all these things of which we accuse him.”
The Jews also joined in the attack, asserting that these things were so.
When the governor motioned for him to speak, Paul answered, “Knowing that you have been a judge of this nation for many years, I cheerfully make my defense concerning myself.
You can confirm that it is no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
They did not find me disputing with anyone or gathering a crowd, whether in the temple, in the synagogues, or in the city.
Nor can they present proof to you of the things they now accuse me of.
But I confess this to you: according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything in accordance with the law and everything written in the prophets,
having hope in God—which these people themselves also await—that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the unrighteous.
For this reason I myself strive always to have a blameless conscience toward God and human beings.
After several years I came to bring alms to my nation and offerings.
While I was engaged in these, they found me purified in the temple, with neither a crowd nor an uproar.
But there were some Jews from Asia who ought to be present before you and bring charges, if they had anything against me.
Or let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council,
except for this one declaration I cried out while standing among them: ‘It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am being judged before you today.’”
Felix, who had more accurate knowledge of the Way, adjourned their case, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.”
He ordered the centurion to keep Paul in custody but grant him some freedom, and not prevent any of his own people from attending to him.
After some days Felix came with his own wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. He summoned Paul and heard him concerning faith in Christ Jesus.
As Paul reasoned about righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became afraid and answered, “Go away for now. When I find an opportunity, I will summon you.”
At the same time he hoped that Paul would give him money. Therefore he summoned him more frequently and conversed with him.
When two years were completed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. Wishing to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul bound.
Three days after arriving in the province, Festus went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
The chief priests and the leading men of the Jews presented their case against Paul to him and urged him,
asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem, while planning an ambush to kill him along the road.
Festus answered that Paul was being kept at Caesarea, and that he himself would soon be going there.
He said, “Let the influential men among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong in the man, let them accuse him.”
After staying among them no more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. The next day he sat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought in.
When he arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious accusations that they could not prove.
Paul made his defense: “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews, against the temple, or against Caesar.”
But Festus, wishing to gain favor with the Jews, answered Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be judged there before me concerning these things?”
Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be judged. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well.

If, then, I am doing wrong and have done anything deserving death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is nothing to their accusations against me, no one can hand me over to them as a favor. I appeal to Caesar.”
Then Festus conferred with his council and answered, “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go.”
After some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived in Caesarea to greet Festus.
While they stayed there for several days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left as a prisoner by Felix.
When I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and elders of the Jews presented their case against him, asking for his condemnation.
I answered them that it is not Roman custom to hand anyone over as a favor before the accused has met his accusers face to face and received an opportunity to defend himself concerning the charge.
So when they gathered here, I made no delay, but on the next day sat on the tribunal and ordered the man brought in.
When his accusers stood up, they brought no charge of the evil things I had expected.
Instead, they had certain disputes with him concerning their own religion and a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul asserted to be alive.
Uncertain how to investigate these matters, I asked whether he wished to go to Jerusalem and be judged there concerning them.
But when Paul appealed to be kept for Augustus’s decision, I ordered him held until I could send him to Caesar.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear the man myself.” He said, “Tomorrow you will hear him.”
The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the audience hall with the tribunes and the city’s prominent men. At Festus’s order, Paul was brought in.

Festus said, “King Agrippa and all you men present with us, you see this man concerning whom the whole multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.
I found that he had done nothing deserving death, but since he himself appealed to Augustus, I decided to send him.

I have nothing certain to write to the sovereign about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after the examination I may have something to write.
For it seems unreasonable to me to send a prisoner without also indicating the charges against him.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “You are permitted to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense:
“Concerning everything of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate to make my defense before you today,
especially since you are familiar with all the Jewish customs and disputes. Therefore I ask you to hear me patiently.
All the Jews know my manner of life from my youth, lived from the beginning among my nation and in Jerusalem.
They have known me from the first, if they are willing to testify, that I lived as a Pharisee according to the strictest party of our religion.
Now I stand on trial because of hope in the promise made by God to our fathers,
which our twelve tribes, earnestly worshiping night and day, hope to attain. It is concerning this hope that I am accused by Jews, O king.
Why do you consider it unbelievable that God raises the dead?
I myself thought that I must do many things against the name of Jesus the Nazarene.
This I did in Jerusalem: I shut up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were being killed, I cast my vote against them.
I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to compel them to blaspheme. In my intense rage against them, I pursued them even to foreign cities.
In this pursuit I was traveling to Damascus with authority and commission from the chief priests,
when at midday, O king, I saw along the road a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those traveling with me.
When we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice speaking to me in the Hebrew language: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me? It is hard for you to kick against goads.’
I said, ‘Who art Thou, Lord?’ The Lord said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But rise and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you a servant and witness of the things in which you have seen Me and those in which I will appear to you,
rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you,

to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from Satan’s authority to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an allotted share among those sanctified by faith in Me.’
Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,
but proclaimed first to those in Damascus and Jerusalem, throughout all the country of Judea, and to the Gentiles that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance.
For these reasons the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.
Having therefore received help from God, I stand to this day, testifying to small and great, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen:
that the Christ would suffer and, as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light both to the people and to the Gentiles.”
As he was making this defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “You are mad, Paul! Your great learning is turning you to madness.”
Paul said, “I am not mad, most excellent Festus, but I speak words of truth and sound judgment.
For the king knows about these things, and I speak freely to him. I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “With so little, you are trying to persuade me to become a Christian.”
Paul said, “Whether with little or with much, I would pray to God that not only you but also all who hear me today might become as I am, except for these bonds.”
The king rose, along with the governor, Bernice, and those seated with them.
After withdrawing, they spoke to one another, saying, “This man is doing nothing deserving death or imprisonment.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
When it was decided that we should sail to Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan cohort.
We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was about to sail to the ports along Asia, and set sail. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.
The next day we put in at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends and receive care.
From there we set sail and sailed under the shelter of Cyprus because the winds were contrary.
We crossed the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia and came to Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing to Italy and put us aboard it.
We sailed slowly for many days and with difficulty came off Cnidus. Since the wind would not permit us to proceed, we sailed under the shelter of Crete off Salmone.
Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.
Much time had passed, and sailing was already dangerous because even the Fast had now gone by. Paul advised them,
saying, “Men, I perceive that the voyage will bring damage and great loss, not only of the cargo and the ship but also of our lives.”
But the centurion was more persuaded by the pilot and the shipowner than by what Paul said.
Since the harbor was unsuitable for wintering, the majority decided to sail from there, hoping somehow to reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest, and winter there.
When a south wind blew gently, they supposed they had gained their purpose, weighed anchor, and sailed close along Crete.
But not long afterward a hurricane wind called Euraquilo rushed down from the island.
The ship was seized and could not face the wind, so we gave way and were driven along.
Running under the shelter of a small island called Cauda, we were barely able to secure the boat.
After hoisting it aboard, they used supports to hold the ship together from beneath. Fearing they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear and were driven along in this way.
As we were violently battered by the storm, the next day they began throwing cargo overboard.
On the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.
When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and a fierce storm kept battering us, all remaining hope of our being saved was taken away.
After a long time without food, Paul stood among them and said, “Men, you ought to have listened to me and not sailed from Crete, and so avoided this damage and loss.
Now I urge you to take courage, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.
For this night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship stood beside me,
saying, ‘Do not fear, Paul. You must stand before Caesar, and look, God has granted you all who sail with you.’
Therefore take courage, men, for I believe God that it will be just as I have been told.
But we must run aground on some island.”
When the fourteenth night came, as we were being driven across the Adria, about midnight the sailors suspected that some land was approaching them.
They took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. After going a little farther, they sounded again and found fifteen fathoms.
Fearing we might run aground somewhere on rocky places, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come.
The sailors sought to flee from the ship and lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they were about to lay out anchors from the bow.
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men remain in the ship, you cannot be saved.”
Then the soldiers cut the boat’s ropes and let it fall away.
As day was about to come, Paul urged everyone to take food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day you have continued waiting without food, taking nothing.
Therefore I urge you to take food, for this is for your safety. Not a hair from the head of any of you will be lost.”
After saying these things, he took bread, gave thanks to God before everyone, broke it, and began to eat.
They all took courage and themselves took food.
There were two hundred and seventy-six persons in all aboard the ship.
When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship by throwing the grain into the sea.
When day came, they did not recognize the land, but noticed a bay with a beach and planned, if they could, to drive the ship onto it.
They cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, while also loosening the lashings of the steering oars. They raised the foresail to the wind and headed for the beach.
But they struck a place between two seas and ran the ship aground. The bow stuck fast and remained immovable, while the stern was breaking apart under the force of the waves.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so that none might swim away and escape.
But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, prevented them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those able to swim to jump overboard first and make for land,
and the rest to follow, some on planks and some on pieces from the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely.
After reaching safety, we learned that the island was called Melite.
The people who did not speak Greek showed us extraordinary kindness. They kindled a fire and welcomed us all because of the rain that had begun and because of the cold.
Paul gathered a bundle of brushwood and put it on the fire. A viper came out because of the heat and fastened onto his hand.

When the people who did not speak Greek saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “This man is certainly a murderer. Although he escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.”
But he shook the creature into the fire and suffered no harm.
They expected him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. After waiting a long time and seeing nothing unusual happen to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.
Near that place were lands belonging to the island’s chief man, named Publius. He welcomed us and hospitably gave us lodging for three days.
Publius’s father lay sick with fevers and dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands upon him, and healed him.
After this happened, the other sick people on the island also came and were healed.
They honored us with many honors, and when we sailed, they supplied what we needed.
After three months we sailed in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered at the island, with the Dioscuri as its emblem.
We put in at Syracuse and stayed three days.
From there we cast off and reached Rhegium. After one day a south wind arose, and on the second day we came to Puteoli.
There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them seven days. And so we came to Rome.
From there the brothers, having heard about us, came to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.
When we entered Rome, Paul was permitted to stay by himself with the soldier guarding him.

After three days he called together the leading Jews. When they gathered, he said to them, “Men, brothers, although I had done nothing against the people or the ancestral customs, I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into Roman hands.
After examining me, they wished to release me, because there was no cause for death in my case.
But when the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar, though I had no accusation to bring against my nation.
For this reason I asked to see you and speak with you, for it is because of Israel’s hope that I wear this chain.”
They said to him, “We have received no letters from Judea about you, nor has any of the brothers who arrived reported or spoken anything evil about you.
But we consider it right to hear from you what you think, for concerning this sect we know that it is opposed everywhere.”

They appointed a day with him and came to his lodging in greater numbers. From morning until evening he explained to them, bearing solemn witness to the kingdom of God and seeking to persuade them concerning Jesus from both the law of Moses and the prophets.
Some were persuaded by what was said, while others did not believe.
Disagreeing with one another, they began to leave after Paul made one statement: “The Holy Spirit spoke well through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers,
saying, ‘Go to this people and say: “You will hear and hear, yet never understand; you will look and look, yet never see.

For this people’s heart has grown dull, their ears have become hard of hearing, and they have closed their eyes, lest they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn back, and I would heal them.”’
Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.”
He remained two whole years in his own rented lodging and welcomed all who came to him,
proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, unhindered.
Paul, a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God,
which He promised beforehand through His prophets in holy Scriptures,
concerning His Son, who came from David’s seed according to the flesh,
who was designated Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,
through whom we received grace and apostleship for the obedience of faith among all the nations for His name,
among whom you also are, called by Jesus Christ:
to all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called as saints: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in the whole world.
For God, whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of His Son, is my witness that I remember you without ceasing,
always in my prayers asking whether somehow now at last I may be granted a way, by the will of God, to come to you.
For I long to see you, to share with you some spiritual gift so that you may be strengthened,
that is, to be encouraged together among you through one another’s faith, both yours and mine.
And I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I often planned to come to you—and was hindered until now—so that I might have some fruit among you also, just as among the other nations.
I am a debtor both to Greeks and to those who do not speak Greek, both to the wise and to the senseless.
Thus, for my part, I am eager to proclaim the gospel also to you who are in Rome.
For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is God’s power for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.
For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written, “But the righteous one will live by faith.”
For God’s wrath is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth in unrighteousness,
because what is known of God is plain among them, for God made it plain to them.
For His invisible qualities, both His eternal power and divinity, have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, understood through the things made, so that they are without excuse,
because, although they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their senseless heart was darkened.
Claiming to be wise, they became foolish,
and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible humanity, and of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things.
Therefore God handed them over, in the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that their bodies would be dishonored among them,
who exchanged the truth of God for the lie, and revered and worshiped the creation instead of the Creator, who is blessed throughout the ages. Amen.
For this reason God handed them over to dishonorable passions; for their females exchanged natural relations for those contrary to nature,

and likewise the males, leaving natural relations with the female, burned in their desire for one another, males with males committing what is shameful and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.
And just as they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, God handed them over to an unfit mind, to do what is not fitting:
filled with all unrighteousness, wickedness, greed, evil; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malice; whisperers,
slanderers, haters of God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents,
without understanding, faithless, without natural affection, merciless;
who, knowing God’s righteous decree, that those who practice such things are worthy of death, not only do them, but also approve those who practice them.
Therefore you are without excuse, O man—whoever you are who judges. For when you judge another, you condemn yourself, because you who judge practice the same things.
And we know that God’s judgment against those who practice such things is according to truth.
But do you think, O man—you who judge those who practice such things and do them yourself—that you will escape God’s judgment?
Or do you despise the wealth of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?
But by your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment,
who will repay each according to his works:
to those who, through perseverance in good work, seek glory and honor and incorruptibility, eternal life;
but to those acting from selfish ambition, who disobey the truth but obey unrighteousness, wrath and fury,
affliction and distress upon every human soul that does evil—the Jew first and also the Greek;
but glory and honor and peace to everyone who does good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.
For there is no partiality with God.
For all who sinned without law will also perish without law; and all who sinned under law will be judged through law.
For it is not the hearers of law who are righteous before God, but the doers of law will be justified.
For whenever Gentiles who do not have law do by nature the things of the law, these, though not having law, are a law to themselves,
who show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness with it, and their reasonings among themselves accusing or even defending,
on the day when God judges people’s secrets according to my gospel through Christ Jesus.
But if you bear the name Jew, and rest upon law and boast in God,
and know His will and approve the things that matter, being instructed from the law,
and are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light to those in darkness,
an instructor of the senseless, a teacher of infants, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
you then who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who proclaim that one must not steal, do you steal?
You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
You who boast in law, do you dishonor God through transgression of the law?
For “the name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of you,” just as it is written.
For circumcision benefits you if you practice law; but if you are a transgressor of law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.
So if the uncircumcised person keeps the law’s righteous requirements, will not his uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision?
And the one uncircumcised by nature who fulfills the law will judge you who, with the written letter and circumcision, are a transgressor of law.
For the Jew is not the one outwardly so, nor is circumcision what is outward in flesh;
but the Jew is the one inwardly so, and circumcision is of the heart, in Spirit, not in letter, whose praise is not from people but from God.
What, then, is the Jew’s advantage, or what is the benefit of circumcision?
Much in every way. First, indeed, because they were entrusted with the oracles of God.
For what if some were unfaithful? Will their unfaithfulness nullify God’s faithfulness?
May it never be! But let God be true, and every human being a liar, just as it is written, “So that Thou mayest be justified in Thy words, and wilt prevail when Thou art judged.”
But if our unrighteousness demonstrates God’s righteousness, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous when He brings wrath? I speak in human terms.
May it never be! For then how will God judge the world?
But if God’s truth abounded through my falsehood to His glory, why am I still judged as a sinner?
And why not say—as we are slandered and as some claim we say—“Let us do evil things so that good things may come”? Their condemnation is just.
What, then? Are we better off? Not at all; for we have already charged both Jews and Greeks with all being under sin,
just as it is written: “There is no righteous one, not even one;
there is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God.
All turned aside; together they became useless. There is no one who shows kindness; there is not even one.
Their throat is an opened tomb; with their tongues they practiced deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips;
their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.
Their feet are swift to pour out blood;
ruin and misery are in their ways,
and the way of peace they did not know.
There is no fear of God before their eyes.”
And we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become answerable to God;
because by works of law no flesh will be justified before Him, for through law comes knowledge of sin.
But now, apart from law, God’s righteousness has been revealed, witnessed by the law and the prophets:
God’s righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. For there is no distinction,
for all sinned and fall short of God’s glory,
being justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
whom God set forth as a propitiation in His blood, through faith, to demonstrate His righteousness because of the passing over of sins committed beforehand,
in God’s forbearance, to demonstrate His righteousness at the present time, so that He may be righteous and justify the one who has faith in Jesus.
Where, then, is boasting? It was excluded. Through what kind of law? Of works? No, but through a law of faith.
For we reckon that a person is justified by faith apart from works of law.
Or is God the God of Jews only? Is He not also of Gentiles? Yes, also of Gentiles,
since God is one, who will justify the circumcised from faith and the uncircumcised through faith.
Do we then nullify law through faith? May it never be! Rather, we establish law.
What, then, shall we say Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has found?
For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast of—but not before God.
For what does the Scripture say? “And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”
Now to the one who works, the wage is not reckoned according to grace, but according to what is owed.
But to the one who does not work, but believes in the One who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness,
just as David also speaks of the blessedness of the person to whom God reckons righteousness apart from works:
“Blessed are those whose lawless deeds were forgiven and whose sins were covered;
blessed is the man whose sin the Lord certainly will not reckon.”
Is this blessedness, then, upon the circumcised, or also upon the uncircumcised? For we say, “Faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness.”
How, then, was it reckoned? While he was circumcised, or uncircumcised? Not while circumcised, but while uncircumcised.

And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while uncircumcised, so that he might be father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness might be reckoned to them also,
and father of the circumcised, to those who are not only circumcised but also walk in the footsteps of the faith our father Abraham had while uncircumcised.
For the promise to Abraham or to his seed that he would be heir of the world was not through law, but through the righteousness of faith.
For if those from law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise has been nullified;
for the law brings wrath, but where there is no law, neither is there transgression.

For this reason it is from faith, so that it may be according to grace, so that the promise may be secure to all the seed—not only to the one from the law, but also to the one from Abraham’s faith. He is father of us all,
just as it is written, “I have made you father of many nations,” before the God whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they are.
Against hope, he believed in hope, so that he might become father of many nations, according to what had been said, “So shall your seed be.”
And without growing weak in faith, he considered his own body, already deadened as it was, being about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah’s womb;
but with regard to God’s promise he did not waver in unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God,
and being fully assured that what He has promised He is also able to do.
Therefore it was also reckoned to him as righteousness.
But “it was reckoned to him” was not written for his sake alone,
but also for our sake, to whom it is to be reckoned, who believe in the One who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead,
who was handed over for our trespasses and was raised for our justification.
Therefore, having been justified from faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand; and we boast in hope of God’s glory.
And not only this, but we also boast in afflictions, knowing that affliction produces perseverance,
and perseverance, proven character, and proven character, hope.
And hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.
For while we were still weak, even then Christ died at the appointed time for the ungodly.
For rarely will someone die for a righteous person; though perhaps for the good person someone even dares to die.
But God demonstrates His own love toward us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Much more, then, having now been justified in His blood, we will be saved through Him from wrath.
For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, much more, having been reconciled, we will be saved in His life.
And not only this, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.
For this reason, just as through one person sin entered the world, and through sin, death, and so death passed to all people, because all sinned—
for before the law came, sin was in the world, but sin is not charged to account when there is no law;
nevertheless death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the One to come.
But the gift is not like the trespass. For if by the one man’s trespass the many died, much more did God’s grace and the gift in the grace of the one Man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many.
And the gift is not like what came through one who sinned; for the judgment from one trespass resulted in condemnation, but the gift from many trespasses resulted in justification.
For if, by the one man’s trespass, death reigned through the one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the One, Jesus Christ.
So then, as through one trespass there was condemnation for all people, so also through one righteous act there is justification of life for all people.
For just as through the disobedience of the one person the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the One the many will be made righteous.
But law came in alongside, so that the trespass might increase; but where sin increased, grace abounded beyond measure,
so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness for eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
What, then, shall we say? Should we remain in sin so that grace may increase?
May it never be! We who died to sin, how will we still live in it?
Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death?
Therefore we were buried with Him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the Father’s glory, so we also might walk in newness of life.
For if we have become united with the likeness of His death, we will also be united with that of His resurrection,
knowing this, that our old self was crucified with Him, so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin;
for the one who died has been justified from sin.
And if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with Him,
knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, no longer dies; death no longer rules over Him.
For the death He died, He died to sin once for all; but the life He lives, He lives to God.
So also reckon yourselves to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.
Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires;
Do not present the parts of your body to sin as weapons of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those alive from the dead, and the parts of your body to God as weapons of righteousness.
For sin will not rule over you, for you are not under law, but under grace.
What, then? Should we sin because we are not under law, but under grace? May it never be!
Do you not know that when you present yourselves to someone as slaves to obey, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin leading to death, or of obedience leading to righteousness?
But thanks be to God that, though you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over;
and, having been set free from sin, you were enslaved to righteousness.

I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented the parts of your body as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to lawlessness, so now present the parts of your body as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification.
For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness.
What fruit, then, did you have at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death.
But now, having been set free from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit leading to sanctification, and the end, eternal life.
For sin’s wages are death, but God’s gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Or do you not know, brothers—for I speak to those who know law—that the law rules over a person for as long as he lives?
For the married woman is bound by law to her living husband; but if the husband dies, she has been released from the law of the husband.

So then, while the husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she belongs to another man; but if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is not an adulteress when she belongs to another man.
So, my brothers, you also were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might belong to Another, the One raised from the dead, so that we might bear fruit for God.
For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions aroused through the law were at work in the parts of our body, to bear fruit for death.
But now we were released from the law, having died to that in which we were held, so that we serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.
What, then, shall we say? Is the law sin? May it never be! Rather, I did not know sin except through law; for I would not have known desire if the law had not said, “You shall not desire.”
But sin, taking opportunity through the commandment, produced every desire in me; for apart from law sin is dead.
And I was once alive apart from law; but when the commandment came, sin came to life,
and I died; and the commandment that was for life proved to bring me death.
For sin, taking opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.
So the law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good.

Did the good, then, become death to me? May it never be! But sin did, so that it might appear as sin, producing death in me through the good, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure.
For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am of flesh, sold under sin.
For I do not understand what I do; for I do not practice what I want, but what I hate, this I do.
But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good.
But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.
For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. For the will is there, but doing what is good is not.
For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, this I practice.
But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.
So I find this law: when I want to do the good, evil is at hand for me.
For I delight in God’s law in my inner self,
but I see another law in the parts of my body, waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin that is in the parts of my body.
Wretched person that I am! Who will rescue me from the body of this death?
Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then I myself, with the mind, serve God’s law, but with the flesh, sin’s law.
So then, there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus.
For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus set you free from the law of sin and death.
For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did: sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and concerning sin, He condemned sin in the flesh,
so that the law’s righteous requirement might be fulfilled in us who walk not according to flesh, but according to Spirit.
For those who are according to flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those according to Spirit, on the things of the Spirit.
For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace,
because the mind of the flesh is hostility toward God; for it does not submit to God’s law, nor indeed can it.
And those who are in flesh cannot please God.
But you are not in flesh, but in Spirit, if indeed God’s Spirit dwells in you. But if anyone does not have Christ’s Spirit, that person does not belong to Him.
But if Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
And if the Spirit of the One who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, the One who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit dwelling in you.
So then, brothers, we are debtors—not to the flesh, to live according to flesh;
for if you live according to flesh, you are going to die; but if by Spirit you put to death the body’s practices, you will live.
For all who are led by God’s Spirit are sons of God.
For you did not receive a spirit of slavery leading again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father.”
The Spirit Himself bears witness with our spirit that we are God’s children.
And if children, then also heirs: heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with Him so that we may also be glorified with Him.
For I reckon that the sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed in us.
For creation eagerly awaits the revealing of God’s sons;
for creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of the One who subjected it, in hope
that creation itself also will be set free from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of God’s children.
For we know that the whole creation groans together and labors in birth pangs together until now;
and not only creation, but we ourselves also, having the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption as sons, the redemption of our body.
For in hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees?
But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with perseverance.
And likewise the Spirit also helps our weakness; for we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit Himself intercedes with groanings beyond words.
And the One who searches hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because He intercedes for saints according to God.
And we know that all things work together for good for those who love God, those who are called according to purpose.
Because those whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He might be firstborn among many brothers;
and those whom He predestined, these He also called; and those whom He called, these He also justified; and those whom He justified, these He also glorified.
What, then, shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?
He who did not spare His own Son, but handed Him over for us all, how will He not also graciously give us all things with Him?
Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? God is the One who justifies.
Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus is the One who died—more than that, was raised—who is also at God’s right hand, who also intercedes for us.
Who will separate us from Christ’s love? Affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?
Just as it is written, “For Thy sake we are put to death all day long; we were reckoned as sheep for slaughter.”
But in all these things we more than conquer through the One who loved us.
For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor rulers, neither things present nor things to come nor powers,
neither height nor depth nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love in Christ Jesus our Lord.
I speak truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness with me in the Holy Spirit,
that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.
For I could wish that I myself were accursed, away from Christ, for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh,
who are Israelites. Theirs are the adoption as sons and the glory and the covenants and the giving of the law and the worship and the promises;
theirs are the fathers, and from them comes the Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed throughout the ages. Amen.
But it is not as though God’s word has failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israel;
neither, because they are Abraham’s seed, are they all children; but, “In Isaac your seed will be called.”
That is, the children of the flesh are not thereby God’s children, but the children of the promise are reckoned as seed.
For this is a word of promise: “At this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son.”
And not only this, but also Rebecca, having conceived by one man, Isaac our father—
for when they had not yet been born or done anything good or bad, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain,
not from works but from the One who calls, it was said to her, “The older will serve the younger,”
just as it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”
What, then, shall we say? Is there unrighteousness with God? May it never be!
For He says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whomever I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whomever I have compassion.”
So then, it depends not on the one who wills, nor on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.
For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might demonstrate My power in you, and so that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”
So then, He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills He hardens.
You will then say to me, “Why, then, does He still find fault? For who has resisted His purpose?”
But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is formed say to the One who formed it, “Why didst Thou make me this way?”
Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?
But what if God, willing to demonstrate wrath and to make His power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction,
and did so to make known the wealth of His glory upon vessels of mercy, which He prepared beforehand for glory,
even us whom He also called, not only from Jews but also from Gentiles?
As He also says in Hosea, “I will call those who are not My people ‘My people,’ and her who is not beloved ‘beloved’;
and it shall come to pass that in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.”
But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel, “Though the number of Israel’s sons be like the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved;
for the Lord will carry out a word on the earth, completing it and cutting it short.”
And just as Isaiah has said beforehand, “Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah.”
What, then, shall we say? That Gentiles who were not pursuing righteousness attained righteousness, namely the righteousness from faith;
but Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not attain law.
Why? Because it was not from faith, but as though from works. They stumbled against the stone of stumbling,
just as it is written, “Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, and the one who believes in Him will not be put to shame.”
Brothers, my heart’s desire and my prayer to God for them are that they may be saved.
For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge;
for, not knowing God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they did not submit to God’s righteousness.
For Christ is the end of law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
For Moses writes about the righteousness from the law: the person who does these things will live by them.
But the righteousness from faith speaks in this way: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’”—that is, to bring Christ down;
or, “‘Who will descend into the abyss?’”—that is, to bring Christ up from the dead.
But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart”—that is, the word of faith that we proclaim.
Because if you confess Jesus as Lord with your mouth, and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved;
for with the heart one believes for righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses for salvation.
For the Scripture says, “Whoever believes in Him shall not be put to shame.”
For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord is Lord of all, being rich toward all who call upon Him;
for “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.”
How, then, are they to call upon One in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in One whom they have not heard? And how are they to hear without someone proclaiming?
And how are they to proclaim unless they are sent? Just as it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those announcing good things!”
But not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, “O Lord, who has believed our report?”
So faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.
But I say, did they not hear? Indeed they did: “Their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world.”
But I say, did Israel not know? First Moses says, “I will make you jealous by what is not a nation; by a senseless nation I will provoke you to anger.”
And Isaiah speaks boldly and says, “I was found among those who did not seek Me; I became known to those who did not ask for Me.”
But concerning Israel He says, “All day long I stretched out My hands toward a disobedient and contrary people.”
I say, then, has God rejected His people? May it never be! For I too am an Israelite, from Abraham’s seed, of Benjamin’s tribe.
God has not rejected His people whom He foreknew. Or do you not know what the Scripture says in the passage about Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel?
“Lord, they killed Thy prophets, they demolished Thy altars, and I alone was left, and they seek my life.”
But what does the divine response say to him? “I left for Myself seven thousand men who did not bend the knee to Baal.”
So then, at the present time also there has come to be a remnant according to an election of grace.
But if by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.
What, then? What Israel seeks, it did not obtain; but the chosen obtained it, and the rest were hardened,
just as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes not to see and ears not to hear, until this very day.”
And David says, “Let their table become a snare and a trap and a stumbling block and a repayment to them;
let their eyes be darkened so as not to see, and bend their back continually.”
I say, then, did they stumble so that they might fall? May it never be! But by their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, to make them jealous.
But if their trespass is the world’s wealth and their loss the Gentiles’ wealth, how much more their fullness!
And I speak to you Gentiles. Insofar as I am an apostle of Gentiles, I glorify my ministry,
if somehow I may make my own flesh jealous and save some of them.
For if their rejection is the world’s reconciliation, what will their acceptance be except life from the dead?
And if the firstfruits are holy, so is the lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.
